title: How To Use ChatGPT To Give Better Feedback In Half The Time
author: Doan Winkel
summary: Winkel gives teachers a workflow for using ChatGPT to speed up developmental feedback on essays and projects without handing over their judgment. His core rule is that AI drafts while the teacher coaches: the teacher sets the learning goals, picks the two or three growth priorities that matter most, and edits every draft before a student sees it. He distinguishes developmental feedback from grading and offers a three-step loop (summarize, diagnose, draft) with a before-and-after example, a reusable Feedback Studio prompt, and a student-facing revision prompt. He also covers failure modes such as overstuffed or vague feedback, privacy guardrails, and a phased rollout. The practical audience is teachers, though the examples are college-level writing.
points: The governing principle is that AI drafts, the teacher coaches, and the relationship stays human, so feedback never goes straight from the model to the student.
A usable test of good feedback is whether a student can say in their own words what to try differently on the next draft.
The three-step loop of summarizing, choosing two or three priorities yourself, then having ChatGPT phrase them keeps the teacher's judgment at the center.
Pasting several students' feedback sketches into a chat to find class-wide patterns turns time-saving into planning for mini lessons.
Listed guardrails include stripping names, following school AI policy, and never letting the tool rewrite student work.
quotes: If your feedback doesn’t change what students do on the next version or the next assignment, it was mostly a waste of your time and theirs. The problem is that we have a system that makes it nearly impossible to give timely, developmental feedback at scale.
The core principle: AI drafts. You coach. The relationship stays human. If you let feedback go straight from AI to student, you break the most important part of the process.
So the rule is simple. ChatGPT can help you think, structure, and phrase feedback. It can’t replace your judgment or your voice.

If a student reads your comments and can’t answer, in their own words, “What exactly should I try differently on my next draft?” the feedback failed, no matter how long it took you to write. AI will not fix that for you.
Overstuffed feedback If the AI draft looks “impressive” because it hits everything the student did wrong, that is a failure. Fix: limit yourself to 2 strengths and 2 growth areas on most work.
Owning these prompts is not the hard part. You can copy them in 10 seconds. The hard part is being honest with yourself about your current feedback patterns.
The critical piece is that your feedback is the anchor. You are still the one defining what “better” looks like. AI is simply helping them see options and possibilities.
